funFacts: A giraffe’s heart can weigh more than 10 kilograms, and it pumps blood all the way up its long neck.
Red pandas use their bushy tails as blankets in cold weather and have a false thumb, an extended wrist bone, that helps them grip bamboo stems.
imageAttribution: Photo: Bernard Landgraf, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: A blobfish's body is mostly a gel-like substance slightly less dense than water, letting it float just above the sea floor without wasting energy swimming.
imageAttribution: Photo: Rachel Caauwe, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: A pangolin's tongue can be longer than its own body, and it retracts into a pouch near its pelvis when not in use.
imageAttribution: Photo: Ari hidayat99, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: A narwhal's tusk is a canine tooth that can grow up to 3 meters long and is packed with nerve endings, possibly helping it sense changes in the water.
imageAttribution: Photo: Gazprom Neft PJSC press service, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: When platypuses were first described to European scientists, many believed the pelt was an elaborate hoax stitched together from other animals.
imageAttribution: Photo: Peter Scheunis, CC BY 1.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: A chameleon's tongue can extend to more than one and a half times its own body length and accelerates faster than a fighter jet.
imageAttribution: Photo: Zeynel Cebeci, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: A tarsier's eyes are so large and fixed in their sockets that it can't roll them at all, its extreme head rotation makes up for it.
imageAttribution: Photo: Seshadri.K.S, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: Axolotls are critically endangered in the wild in Mexico, even though they're one of the most common amphibians kept in captivity worldwide.
imageAttribution: Photo: Amandasofiarana, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: Sloths only leave their trees to go to the bathroom about once a week, and the trip can be dangerous since it's when they're most vulnerable to predators.
imageAttribution: Photo: Krunal Desai, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: Aardvarks can seal their nostrils shut to keep dust and insects out while digging or eating termites.
imageAttribution: Photo: Nick Helme, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: Male seahorses carry fertilized eggs in a specialized pouch and give birth to fully-formed babies, one of the only examples of male pregnancy in the animal kingdom.
imageAttribution: Photo: FASTILY, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: A chinchilla's fur is so tightly packed that fleas can't survive in it, since there's no room for them to move around.
imageAttribution: Photo: Trurl66, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: An octopus can change both the color and texture of its skin in less than a second to blend almost perfectly into its surroundings.
imageAttribution: Photo: Martijn Klijnstra, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: Despite its tough shell, this creature is astonishingly small — adults typically measure under 5 inches long and weigh about as much as a bar of soap. It has only one living relative in its entire subfamily, the greater version of itself.
imageAttribution: Photo: Cliff, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: The vivid blue color of this bird's feet actually comes from its diet, and the brighter the hue, the more attractive it is to potential mates. Females are noticeably larger than males, growing up to 90 cm long with a wingspan reaching 1.5 meters.
imageAttribution: Photo: SantiagoGG, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: Flamingos get their pink color from pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat, and in captivity they can turn pale without the right diet.
imageAttribution: Photo: Charles J. Sharp, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

funFacts: Despite its size, the keel-billed toucan's colorful bill is surprisingly light. It's officially the national bird of Belize, and its diet is far from picky, ranging from fruit and insects to lizards, snakes, and even other birds' eggs.
imageAttribution: Photo: Ttschleuder, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons
